newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - US managers unimpressed by perky JGBs.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US managers unimpressed by perky JGBs.

text.p: Japanese government bonds looked like a bargain after last week's anemic "Tankan" report squashed hopes for a rate hike in Japan this year.
But global investors said the JGB rally that followed the report presents an opportunity to pare Japanese holdings and load up on convergence trades in Europe and among dollar-block currencies.
"Over the last year or two it's been the sell of a generation," Michael Perelstein, portfolio manager of MainStay International Fund, said of the 10-year JGB.
The JGB currently yields just under 3.0 percent.
Traders and investors had been looking for JGB yields to head back up to 3.5 percent or maybe higher. But the release of Japan's quarterly corporate survey changed the market's outlook.
The key diffusion index for major manufacturers fell to minus seven in August from minus three in May. Analysts had been expecting a slight rise.

With Japanese interest rates pegged at record low levels and the Bank of Japan likely to delay any rate hike in the face of tepid economic confidence, investors' focus is on markets where proactive central bank policy can complement bond-investment strategy.
In addition, global growth over the next year or so should benefit the commodity-based economies of some dollar-block markets, said one fund manager.
Speculation on future interest rate cuts may also facilitate capital flows into these currencies.

"Because of the weak 'Tankan' report, the feeling is that Japan's interest rate hike is on the back burner," said Charles Ovis, director of global capital markets at Everen Securities Inc. "So, from an interest rate differential perspective, countries like the U.S., Australia and New Zealand hold greater short-term interest."
In addition, the bond markets in Australia and New Zealand will probably experience sizable interest rate reductions over the next six-to-nine months, he added.

Although the premiums that 10-year Australian, New Zealand and Canadian government bond yields enjoy over U.S. Treasury notes have diminished, investment managers said the spreads could narrow further.

From the non-U.S. perspective, Perelstein suggests turning to Europe. "The most prudent thing one can do is to prune holdings from Japan. Europe is the natural home for a lot of these holdings because the central banks certainly have room to reduce rates; if not in Germany, then in the periphery of Europe."
The recent stumble of currencies like the lira and French franc on the path towards European currency union have not chased steadfast investors away from Europe.

The political will to increase revenues to meet fiscal targets and thus gain entry to the single currency in Europe should keep interest rates in non-core European countries on a downward trajectory, strategists said.

Regardless of whether future German interest rate cuts are in the pipeline after the Bundesbank cut its repo to a record-low 3.0 percent on August 22, some investors see profit potential as differentials between interest rates in Germany and some non-core European countries narrow.

"To the extent bonds still offer this premium over Germany, a significant proportion of this risk continues to be priced in," said Ed Vaimberg, global fixed income portfolio manager at Bear Stearns and Co Inc.
Vaimberg said his portfolio is underweight core European currencies such as Germany, Belgium, France and the Netherlands and overweight Sweden, Ireland and Denmark.
He has watched spreads between 10-year Swedish goverment bonds and German bunds contract from about 210 basis points to 160, before widening out again recently.
"In Sweden/Germany as a reference point, I'm still looking for further compression from say 175 to 125," Vaimberg added.

And MainStay's Perelstein summed up a major incentive: "You are going to be having central banks (in peripheral European countries) behind you as a bond investor rather than having to fight them, as you will in Japan."
